subject: maths
title: Chapter 9 · Test 3
summary: A 15-question test on Year 9 Chapter 9: histograms and stem-and-leaf plots, shape of distributions, centre and spread, two-step chance experiments and tree diagrams.
body:
This test covers Chapter 9, Probability and statistics: histograms and stem-and-leaf plots, the shape of data distributions, measures of centre and spread, two-step chance experiments and tree diagrams.

## How to do this test

- **Time:** about 25 minutes.
- **Conditions:** no notes and no calculator unless the question says. Show your working on paper.
- **Diagrams:** many questions have a histogram, table of outcomes or tree diagram — read the numbers on it carefully.
- **Levels:** 4 easy, 5 medium, 4 hard and 2 challenge questions.
- **After marking:** for each question you got wrong, go back to the lesson it came from and redo its worked examples. Then try another Chapter 9 test — each one has different questions on the same skills.

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the times (minutes) 36 customers spent in a shop. How many customers were in the class 30 to less than 40 minutes?
questions.explanation: The bar from 30 to 40 reaches a height of 7. The neighbouring bar (3) is for the next class.
steps: Find the bar that starts at 30 and ends at 40.
Read its height on the frequency axis: 7.

mistakes.A: Step 1: that is the bar for 40 to less than 50. Find the bar that starts at 30.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 30 is a class boundary on the horizontal axis. Read the bar’s height on the frequency axis.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 12 adds every bar from 30 upwards. Read just the one bar from 30 to 40.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of the times (minutes) 36 customers spent in a shop, with class boundaries 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 and frequencies 4, 8, 12, 7, 3, 2

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the heights (cm) of 50 Year 9 students. Which word best describes the shape of the distribution?
questions.explanation: It is symmetric: it has one peak in the middle and falls away evenly on both sides. Look at the whole display, not just one bar.
steps: Look for the peak (or peaks) and for any long tail.
Here it has one peak in the middle and falls away evenly on both sides, so it is symmetric.

mistakes.B: Step 1: the bars fall away evenly on both sides of the middle — there is no long tail on one side.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the bars fall away evenly on both sides of the middle — there is no long tail on one side.
mistakes.D: Step 1: there is only one peak, in the middle. Bimodal needs two clear peaks.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of the heights (cm) of 50 Year 9 students, with class boundaries 145, 150, 155, 160, 165, 170, 175, 180 and frequencies 2, 5, 10, 16, 10, 5, 2

questions.prompt: The number of goals scored in 7 hockey games: 5, 12, 8, 3, 14, 6, 15. What is the median?
questions.explanation: In order: 3, 5, 6, 8, 12, 14, 15. The middle (4th) value is 8. Taking the middle of the unordered list gives 3, which is wrong.
steps: 7 values, so the median is the 4th: 8.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 3 is the middle of the list as written. Put the values in order first.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 9 is the mean (total ÷ 7). The median is the middle value of the ordered list.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 12 is the range (15 − 3). The median is the middle value.

questions.prompt: A coin is tossed and a card is drawn from 8 cards numbered 1 to 8. How many different outcomes are there?
questions.explanation: Every one of the 2 outcomes of the first step can pair with every one of the 8 outcomes of the second: 2 × 8 = 16. Adding (10) misses most of the pairs.
steps: Step 1 has 2 outcomes and step 2 has 8.

mistakes.A: Step 2: you added 2 + 8. Each of the 2 first results pairs with each of the 8 second results, so multiply.
mistakes.B: Step 1: 8 counts only the cards. Each card can come with a head or a tail.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 8 × 8 uses the cards twice. The coin has only 2 outcomes.

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the ages of 45 people at a gym class. How many were 35 years or more?
questions.explanation: The bars from 35 upwards have heights 10 + 7 + 5 + 3 = 25. Using only the first of those bars (10) misses the rest.
steps: "35 or more" means every bar that starts at 35 or higher.

mistakes.B: Step 1: 10 is only the bar from 35 to 45. Every bar further right is also "35 or more".
mistakes.C: Step 1: you included the bar from 25 to 35. Start at the bar that begins at 35.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 20 counts the values LESS than 35. Add the bars from 35 upwards.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of the ages of 45 people at a gym class, with class boundaries 15, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65, 75 and frequencies 8, 12, 10, 7, 5, 3

questions.prompt: The masses (g) of 8 apples: 73, 50, 64, 61, 79, 52, 66, 57. Find the interquartile range.
questions.explanation: Ordered: 50, 52, 57, 61, 64, 66, 73, 79. Q1 = (52 + 57) ÷ 2 = 54.5 and Q3 = (66 + 73) ÷ 2 = 69.5, so IQR = 15. The range (29) uses the extremes instead.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 29 is the range (79 − 50). The IQR is Q3 − Q1.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 62.5 is the median of the whole set. The IQR is the difference between the quartiles.
mistakes.D: Step 2: each half has 4 values, so its median is the AVERAGE of its two middle values, not one of them.

questions.prompt: Cards 2, 3, 5 and 7 are in a bag. Two are drawn WITHOUT replacement and their numbers are multiplied. The table shows the products (crossed-out cells are impossible). What is the probability that the product is greater than 10?
questions.explanation: Of the 12 possible cells, the products 14, 15, 21 and 35 each appear twice — 8 cells — so P = 8/12 = 2/3. Counting the diagonal too gives 10/16 = 5/8.
steps: Possible outcomes: 4 × 3 = 12 (the diagonal is crossed out).
Products greater than 10: 14, 15, 21, 35, each in 2 cells — 8 cells.

mistakes.A: Step 1: you included the crossed-out diagonal (like 5 × 5). Without replacement a card can’t be drawn twice.
mistakes.B: Step 1: the count of 8 is right, but the total is 12 possible cells, not 16.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 3 × 5 and 5 × 3 are different cells. Count both orders.

questions.diagram_alt: A 4 by 4 table of products of two cards (2, 3, 5, 7) drawn without replacement; the diagonal is crossed out and the other cells show 6, 10, 14, 15, 21 and 35, each twice

questions.prompt: A fair die is rolled twice. The tree diagram shows "6" and "not 6" for each roll. What is the probability of rolling a 6 both times?
questions.explanation: Two sixes means 6 AND 6, so multiply along the path: 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36. Adding gives 1/3, which is far too likely.

mistakes.B: Step 2: along a path you multiply, not add: 1/6 × 1/6.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 1/6 is only the first roll. Both rolls must be 6.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 1/6 × 5/6 is a 6 then NOT a 6. Follow the 6–6 path.

questions.diagram_alt: A tree diagram with 6 at 1/6 and Not 6 at 5/6 for the first roll, and the same two branches again after each

questions.prompt: A data set has a mean of 42 and a median of 35. Which shape is it most likely to have?

options.D: It is impossible to say anything about the shape

questions.explanation: The mean (42) is greater than the median (35), so some large values are pulling the mean up — a tail to the right, positively skewed.
steps: The mean is pulled towards the long tail; the median hardly moves.
Mean (42) greater than median (35) → tail towards large values → positively skewed.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the mean is pulled towards the tail. Mean ABOVE median means the tail points to the larger values: positive.
mistakes.C: Step 1: in a symmetric distribution the mean and median are about equal. These differ by 7.
mistakes.D: Step 1: comparing the mean and median does give a clue: the mean follows the tail.

questions.prompt: The histogram shows the battery life (hours) of 50 phones. What percentage of them were 14 hours or more?
questions.explanation: 7 + 3 = 10 out of 50, and 10 ÷ 50 × 100 = 20%. Giving 10% forgets to divide by the total.
steps: Bars that are 14 hours or more: 7 + 3 = 10.

mistakes.B: Step 1: you used only one bar (7). Include every bar that is 14 hours or more.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 10 is the NUMBER of them. Divide by the total of 50 and multiply by 100.
mistakes.D: Step 1: you included one bar too many. Check where "14 hours or more" starts and stops on the horizontal axis.

questions.diagram_alt: A histogram of the battery life (hours) of 50 phones, with class boundaries 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18 and frequencies 4, 9, 15, 12, 7, 3

questions.prompt: 4 scores have a mean of 7.5. 3 of them are 6, 9, 8. What is the last one?
questions.explanation: All 4 must total 7.5 × 4 = 30; the known ones total 23, so the last is 30 − 23 = 7. Guessing it equals the mean is the common slip.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the missing value does not have to equal the mean. Use total = mean × number of values.
mistakes.C: Step 1: there are 4 values, so the total is 7.5 × 4, not 7.5 × 3.
mistakes.D: Step 1: that is the mean of the 3 known values. Find the total needed for all 4.

questions.prompt: Ten cards are numbered 1 to 10. Two cards are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both numbers are even?
questions.explanation: P(even, even) = 5/10 × 4/9 = 20/90 = 2/9. 1/4 forgets that the first even card is not replaced.
steps: First card: 5 even out of 10, so 5/10.
Second card: 4 even out of the 9 left, so 4/9.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 1/2 × 1/2 is WITH replacement. After one even card is taken, only 4 of the 9 left are even.
mistakes.B: Step 2: the denominator 9 is right, but one even card is gone, so only 4 evens remain, not 5.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 1/2 is only the first card. Both cards must be even — multiply by the second branch.

questions.prompt: A president and a secretary are chosen at random from five people: A, B, C, D and E (no one can do both). Using the table, what is the probability that both A and E are chosen (in either job)?
questions.explanation: There are 5 × 4 = 20 possible cells and both A and E are chosen in AE and EA, so P = 2/20 = 1/10. Counting just one order gives 1/20.
steps: Cells with both A and E: AE and EA — 2 cells.

mistakes.A: Step 1: you allowed the same person to hold both jobs (25 cells). Without the diagonal there are 20 cells.
mistakes.B: Step 2: AE and EA are different cells (A president or E president). Count both.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 2/5 is the chance that A or E is president. Both of them must be chosen.

questions.diagram_alt: A 5 by 5 table with president A to E down the side and secretary A to E across the top; the diagonal is crossed out and the other 20 cells show pairs such as AB and BA

questions.prompt: Data: 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7, 30. The value 30 was a typing error and should be 8. After fixing it, what happens to the mean and median?

options.B: The mean falls by about 3.1; the median stays at 5
options.C: The mean stays the same; the median falls
options.D: The mean falls by 22; the median stays at 5

questions.explanation: The total drops by 30 − 8 = 22, so the mean drops by 22 ÷ 7 ≈ 3.1 (from about 8.4 to about 5.3). The 4th value is still 5, so the median does not move.
steps: The ordered list is still 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7, … so the median (4th value) stays 5.

mistakes.A: Step 3: the median is still the 4th of 7 ordered values, which is 5 both times.
mistakes.C: Step 2: the total drops by 22, so the mean must change. The middle value does not.
mistakes.D: Step 2: the TOTAL falls by 22. Divide by the 7 values to see how much the mean falls.

questions.prompt: A fair coin is tossed three times. What is the probability of getting at least one head?
questions.explanation: The only path with no heads is TTT, with probability 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8, so P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8.
steps: A three-stage tree has 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 equally likely paths.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 3/8 is EXACTLY one head. "At least one" also includes two or three heads.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 1/8 is the chance of NO heads (TTT). Subtract it from 1.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 0, 1, 2 and 3 heads are not equally likely. Use the 8 equally likely paths.
